events.title: Annapolis Jazz & Roots Festival
events.description: Annapolis Jazz & Roots is launching its fifth festival on the scenic shores of the Chesapeake Bay. Events combine music, art, poetry and history on two weekends, November 6-15. Based in the maritime community of Eastport, the festival includes eight venues in nearby neighborhoods. Each has its own distinct character and charm. Festival goers can visit centuries old buildings, take in restorative bay views and stroll the tree-lined streets of the historic Maryland city. THEME AND HIGHLIGHTS The 2026 theme “New World Music: Centuries of Sound” will be brought home by international and regional performers. An adventurous lineup includes programs rooted in history and culture from colonial days to modern times. Trace the evolution of music and culture since the days Indigenous tribes walked the forests and rode the waters. Gain new insights into the startling history and legacy of slavery and indenture in Maryland; delve into the soulful roots of jazz, and celebrate the changing color of sound in America. Events are free or require modest admission, and all but two venues offer free onsite parking. Reservations are strongly advised for all events. Tickets are sold through instantseats.com. WEEKEND ONE Opening Night takes place Friday, November 6 at 7:00 p.m. at St. Luke’s Episcopal Church in Eastport. Jazz lovers will appreciate how the intimacy and beautiful acoustics of the venue elevate the listening experience when the Muneer Nasser Band performs. Trumpeter Muneer Nasser was exposed to great music by his father, jazz bassist Jamil Nasser. This concert pays homage to three legendary musicians born in 1926: John Coltrane, Miles Davis and Randy Weston. Their brave explorations led to seismic shifts in the sonic landscape and continue to resonate around the globe. On Saturday at 11:00 a.m. visit Eastport-Annapolis Neck Library to gain new insights into slavery and indenture in colonial times. events.description: A favorite for 50 years and a wonderful introduction to so much of what Annapolis offers! Stroll through the historic district with your colonial-attired guide. events.title: Billy Price Band
events.description: 6:00pm • $25 • Tickets on Eventbrite and at the door if still available Billy Price Band Billy Price Band brings soul-blues royalty to Hank Dietle’s Tavern. Price first earned national attention as Roy Buchanan’s vocalist, appearing on Buchanan’s That’s What I’m Here For and Live Stock . Since then, the Pittsburgh singer has built a remarkable catalog spanning 21 albums, CDs, and DVDs—delivering a signature blend of deep soul, blues grit, and first-rate band. His acclaimed collaboration with the late Otis Clay, This Time for Real , won the 2016 Blues Music Award for Best Soul Blues Album. Price has also earned 11 Blues Music Award nominations between 2019 and 2025, received the 2024 Bluebird Reviews Lifetime Career Award in the U.K., and saw his 2024 release Person of Interest nominated for 2025 BMAs in both Soul Blues Album and Album of the Year. Now, Billy returns with the Billy Price Band and their new GetHip release, Random Madness . Recorded in Pittsburgh and released May 1, 2026, the album features 11 new songs co-written by Price and produced by Grammy-winning drummer Tony Braunagel. Backed by Dave Dodd on drums, Tom Valentine on bass, Ian Arthurs on guitar, Jim Britton on keyboards, Eric Spaulding on sax, and Joe Herndon on trumpet, the Billy Price Band brings seasoned musicianship, roaring horns, and irresistible soul-blues energy to one of the area’s most intimate rooms. Order Billy's new album "Random Madness " YouTube • Live @Hank Dietle’s Tavern

events.title: Bison: Standing Strong
events.address: 10th St. & Constitution Ave., NW, Washington, DC 20560
events.description: Explore the remarkable story of bison. These iconic animals shaped North American landscapes for more than 100,000 years and anchored Indigenous lifeways for generations. Pushed to the brink of extinction in the 19th century, bison survived thanks to dedicated conservation efforts. Today, they stand strong as an enduring symbol of survival and resilience. The Bison: Standing Strong exhibit invites you into this incredible journey. Explore a full-sized bull bison specimen, the six-foot-wide skull of an ancient bison ancestor, an immersive soundscape, multimedia, cutting-edge scientific research, and Native objects and stories shared in collaboration with community members. Experience the deep history of America’s national mammal and discover the hopeful future being built for generations to come.

Bronze Bison: Exhibit
events.address: 10th St. & Constitution Ave., NW, Washington, DC 20560
events.description: More than 100 years ago, real bison grazed outside the Smithsonian Castle building. Bison are returning in a bold new way! Three larger-than-life bronze bison, created by sculptor Gary Staab, find a permanent home outside the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History. These towering sculptures of a bull, cow, and calf are at 125 percent scale and modeled after taxidermy specimens seen at the Smithsonian between 1888 and 1957. The original bison diorama introduced generations of visitors to an animal and a prairie landscape they had never seen and helped spark the bison conservation movement. The new bison bronzes will welcome visitors from around the world and celebrate America’s national mammal. Gift of Naoma Tate and the family of Hal Tate.

events.title: Caroline, or Change the Musical
events.description: 8 performances | October 31 and November 6*, 7, 13, and 14 at 7:30pm | November 1, 8, and 15 at 2:00pm *Friday, November 6 will include ASL interpretation and free tickets for Montgomery County residents! Full information at www.r-m-t.org/caroline-or-change Set in one of the most pivotal times in America’s history, the Tony-nominated Caroline, or Change is riveting, moving and awe-inspiring. Featuring a virtuosic score by Jeanine Tesori (Shrek The Musical, Thoroughly Modern Millie), it blends blues, gospel and traditional Jewish melodies, creating a breathtaking medium for Kushner’s provocative and personal story. ​ In 1963, the Gellman family and their African-American maid, Caroline, live in sleepy Lake Charles, Louisiana. Caroline is drifting through life as a single mother of four working in a service job to a white family. A fragile, yet beautiful friendship develops between the young Gellman son, Noah, and Caroline. Noah’s stepmother, Rose, unable to give Caroline a raise, tells Caroline that she may keep the money that Noah leaves in his pockets. Caroline balks and refuses to take money from a child but her own children desperately need food, clothing and shoes. Outside of the laundry room, some of the greatest social advancements that the country has seen are being set in motion, and change is knocking on the door. ​ Caroline, or Change is a story that must be shared and will touch hearts. It is a story that will open minds. It is a story that will change theatergoers

events.title: Cinema Art Bethesda: How to Divorce During the War
events.description: As part of its monthly film screening series, Cinema Art Bethesda is pleased to present Andrius Blaževičius’s award-winning 2026 film. Vilnius, Lithuania, 2022. High-flying executive Marija chooses the worst possible moment to inform her husband Vytas she wants a divorce: just one day before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Suddenly, the couple must navigate the process of separation in tandem with a refugee crisis as well as a mid-life crisis. A struggling film director, Vytas is forced to move in with his Russophile parents, while Marija sees the war impacting both her business and her home life. As the reason for the divorce becomes clear, the dissolution of Marija’s and Vytas’ marriage creates conflicts and opportunities for both of them while also affecting their ever-observant young daughter Dovile. Packed with surprises, Blaževičius’s family drama depicts the fallout of a marriage against the backdrop of extraordinary events with humor and compassion. How to Divorce During the War ( Skyrybos karo metu ) is 1 hour 48 minutes long and in Lithuanian, English, Ukrainian, and Russian with English subtitles. This film is not rated. Free bagels, coffee, and tea. Discussion to follow.

events.title: Civil War History in Oakton and Vienna
events.description: Greater Oakton Community Association invites history enthusiasts to join a narrated historic bus tour led by acclaimed local historian Jim Lewis on from 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. Please arrive at 9:00 a.m. at Oakton Community Park at 2841 Hunter Mill Road (next to the old schoolhouse and roundabout) for Jim Lewis's opening comments, then board the bus for departure by 9:30 a.m. The tour will end at 1:00 p.m. This 3.5-hour journey spans Fairfax County's history from its formation in 1742 through the early 1900s, focusing on sites primarily on or just off Hunter Mill Road. Participants hear stories of where the old mills and roads were located and learn about famed military figures (particularly from the Civil War era) and colorful residents who graced the area. Numerous period photographs support the narrative, bringing history to life. Walking requirements are minimal, although one segment involves going down a slight grassy decline. Maryland Double Deckers, in partnership with Heritage Frederick, invites you to experience Frederick’s historic buildings on the special Elevated Architecture tour. events.title: Entertainment Nation

events.description: Entertainment has the power to captivate, inspire and transform us. It brings us together. We share it when we spontaneously recite lines from a favorite movie, dance to the same groove or recreate a national sports moment on a neighborhood street. It can also spur critical conversations, expose divides, and foster important historical change. Through the National Museum of American History’s extraordinary collection of theater, music, sports, movie and television objects, the exhibition features a powerful, ever-changing selection of objects and interactive experiences. Through the objects and their stories, the exhibition explores how, for more than 150 years, entertainment has provided a forum for important national conversations about who we are, and who we want to be.

events.title: Franni Cash: Here I Am Tour 2026
events.description: For fans of We The Kingdom, Jamie MacDonald, and CAIN Franni Cash doesn’t just say what’s on her mind; she sings it as loudly as possible. The GRAMMY® Award-nominated Platinum singer, songwriter, and producer isn’t afraid to speak truth to power, tear down false idols, or point out hypocrisy when it comes to religion, church, or “Country Club Christians” —as she does on the likes of “Church Clothes” and “Koolaid. ” Opening up about her doubts, questions, and struggles in conversation, at shows, and on tape has made her faith stronger and given her music meaning. To paint a personal picture, she chooses to sonically color outside of the lines. The songstress spikes soulful-style hooks with rock ‘n’ roll attitude, bringing soul to Americana-style instrumentation, as she laces a sly sense of humor into the fabric of her unapologetic storytelling. She even co-opts and reclaims words and phrases once used to lambast her (such as “Jezebel”) for her own. Now, Franni declares who she is on her 2026 debut LP , Here I Am. She intentionally arranged and sequenced this 13-track body of work to tell her story in the order that she wanted to. Over the course of the journey, she looked back on how far she’s come. “I don’t know anybody who hasn’t had a problem with religion at some point, ” she observes. “Just because you’ve been burned by a church or by broken people in the church, it doesn’t mean you can’t have faith. To me, that’s what this record is about. It’s about coming back to music and true faith in a relationship with God, addressing the pain and ultimately seeking to heal from it. ” Discover More Attractions in #FXVA

events.title: Friends Gather Here: A Legacy of Two Communities at Woodlawn
events.description: Friends Gather Here: A Legacy of Two Communities at Woodlawn explores the powerful history of Quaker families who came to Woodlawn to establish an antislavery community rooted in equality and nonviolence. Through innovative farming and free labor, they sought to demonstrate an alternative to slavery in Virginia, settling alongside a small, established free Black community already living in the area. This exhibit examines the parallel lives, shared aspirations, and evolving relationships between these neighboring communities. As part of the Virginia 250th commemoration, Friends Gather Here invites us to reflect on this quiet revolution and examine our nation’s foundational ideals. events.title: Gallery B Presents “Intersections | Realism & Abstraction”
events.description: “ INTERSECTIONS ⎸ Realism & Abstraction” is a group exhibition featuring four artists – Lawrence Chandler, Angela Iovino, Ariana Progri, and Ravi Raman – with distinct art styles in conversation with each other, showing that even the most realistic art is a form of abstraction (a reduction of reality) and that abstract art can hold elements of structural, grounded reality. Instead of treating realism and abstraction as binary opposites, works in the exhibition also intersect both worlds, showcasing how different artists navigate the spectrum between the two styles. Viewers not only will see realistic figures and recognizable subjects dissolving into, or emerging from abstract backgrounds, but also the use of bold brushstrokes, form, color, and textures to convey emotion rather than literal details.

events.title: Hiking Through America's History on the Crossing Trail
events.description: Did you know that part of the Washington-Rochambeau Revolutionary Route National Historic Trail passes through Prince William Forest Park? Take a hike through history at Prince William Forest Park on the Crossing Trail, which follows part of the route where, in 1781, General Rochambeau's French Army and General Washington's Continental Army marched troops south from New York to fight the British Army in Yorktown, VA during the Revolutionary War. Celebrate the 250th anniversary of American Independence by following in the footsteps of these armies as you learn about travel in the 1700s along this one and a half mile trail. events.description: Get the Holidays started indoors by joining us on Sunday, November 8th at 1 pm or on Saturday November 14th at 3 pm for a Paperwhite Forcing Workshop! Grow your own fragrant winter flowers! During this hands-on workshop, you’ll discover why paperwhites (a no-chill narcissus/daffodil) have been a holiday staple for generations, how these clever bulbs know it’s time to bloom, and the simple secrets to forcing them indoors for Christmas, New Year’s, or mid-winter cheer. You’ll plant your own pot of paperwhites to take home - ready to perfume your house in just a few weeks - and leave knowing exactly how to keep them happy while they grow, the little tricks that keep the stems from flopping over like they’ve had one too many eggnogs, and what to do once the blooms fade. Perfect for beginners, plant lovers, and anyone who wants a little living magic on the windowsill through the gloomy winter months! From their history to their biology, come learn how these willing winter performers let us coax their beauty out this time of year. Grab your ticket before their gone, and start your holiday prep now!

events.title: In Pursuit of Life, Liberty & Happiness
events.address: 14th Street and Constitution Avenue, N.W., Washington, DC 20560
events.description: The Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History will lead the nation’s 250th anniversary celebrations with a bold, immersive exhibition exploring the ideals of the Declaration of Independence. In Pursuit of Life, Liberty & Happiness will span three floors and 300,000 square feet, featuring 250 significant objects, including the desk Jefferson used to draft the Declaration of Independence. Another noteworthy artifact is the only surviving ship of the early U.S. Navy, the gunboat Philadelphia . This National Historic Landmark helped stall British forces and now will undergo an on-site conservation to preserve it for future generations. Visitors and online audiences can engage with both the triumphs and challenges of America’s journey through a year-long series of dynamic programs, from hands-on activities and theatrical performances to educational tools and virtual field trips for classrooms across the country. The museum's Semiquincentennial exhibitions and events begin in the spring of 2026, welcoming all Americans to reflect on the enduring and sometimes delayed or denied promises that surround the ongoing pursuit of life, liberty and happiness.

Sisters Rebecca and Katherine began their harmonious journey at birth, with writing, creating, and sculpting sound as a family birthright and music a family affair. The Infamous Holman Sisters feature the incredible melodic and sweeping musical stylings of Miss Dawn Cunningham on violin. Her textured layering and emotional melodies dynamically infuse and perfectly complement both original ballads and fan favorites. Dawn's lifelong devotion to her craft is instantaneously recognizable from note one, completing this triad of feminine southern energy and charm. This evening celebrates authentic Appalachian traditions, sibling harmonies, and exceptional musicianship in Fairfax County, Virginia. Admission is $25 plus tax per performance; full six-concert season tickets are $135 plus tax. The Infamous Holman Sisters performance combines heartfelt vocals, skilled instrumentation, and southern heritage. Discover More Attractions in #FXVA

events.title: Las Migas
events.description: The Barcelona quartet Las Migas was founded in 2004 by classically trained musicians from the Escola Superior de Música de Catalunya, united by a shared passion for Spanish music. Six albums and four Latin Grammy nominations later—including two Best Flamenco Album wins for Libres (2022) and Flamencas (2025)—the group continues to push the boundaries of flamenco, blending traditional Spanish folk–inspired guitar with pop and hip-hop influences. Founding member Marta Robles is joined by Paula Rodríguez, Laura Pacios, and Alicia Grillo, whose roots span Seville, Cataluña, La Mancha, and Galicia. Their sound draws on these regional traditions alongside Cuban rumba, while their songwriting centers a woman’s perspective. The group’s songs of liberation have earned them an international audience and strong connections within Spanish and Latin American LGBTQ+ communities.

Instructors will walk through the setup, practice hands together, and guide you step-by-step so you feel comfortable joining the game. No experience needed-just bring your curiosity! events.title: Miguel Braceli: UNBURIAL (exhibition)
events.address: St. John's College, 60 College Avenue, Annapolis, MD 21401
events.description: Unburial treats absence as a site for learning and reflection. The void left by the Liberty Tree becomes more than metaphor: an art intervention transforms it into a place to be repurposed and reclaimed through rituals and celebrations that probe what freedom means today. On the front lawn, where the Liberty Tree once stood, the artist Miguel Braceli has installed a 40'-diameter circle of cemetery vases filled with common wildflowers. It calls attention to the tree's absence and reclaims it as a tree for all people, not just the privileged and elite (e.g., the Sons of Liberty and the four Annapolis signers of the Declaration of Independence). In the museum, Braceli, with the help of a team of fabricators, created three enormous murals and two other works. The murals perform an autopsy of the tree. The largest multiplies the tulip poplar's distinctive leaf shape across a 33'-long wall in a wind-swept swirl of energy (the leaves were made from stencils of the Liberty Tree scion's actual leaves). A second mural abstracts the tree's tangled root system into a water-bearing drawing (using PVC tubing) that sprouts purple carnations. The third mural's subject is the tree's massive trunk, which was cut to pieces in 1999, with much of the wood later finding commemorative as Liberty Tree guitars, conference tables, and bible boxes. Onto nine chalkboards, Braceli has mounted nine pieces of raw wood, each supporting live orchids. What can we learn anew from this tree?, it seems to ask. The two other works urge us to turn away from nation-state identities and to look and listen more closely to nature. A sculptural ear is mounted onto the red silhouette of a rose petal, borrowed from the work of Columbia-born, Venezuela-based artist Roberto Obregoń. Nearby, a flag of yellow roses hangs from a flagpole that has been fabricated from a branch. Admission & Hours Free & open to the public Wednesday, Thursday, Saturday, and Sunday, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Open Friday, 12 to 7:30 p.m. Parking

events.title: Monocacy Battlefield Tour
events.description: The Battle that Saved Washington Battlefields have a remarkable habit of looking peaceful. You’d never guess they were once full of people making spectacularly bad days for one another. On July 9, 1864, Monocacy National Battlefield became the setting for the battle remembered as the “Battle That Saved Washington.” By delaying the Confederate advance on the nation’s capital, the Union forces bought precious time for Washington’s defenses, making Monocacy one of the Civil War’s most significant, and perhaps most underestimated, battlefields. Beginning at the Monocacy Battlefield Visitor Center , we’ll journey through the battlefield with a National Park Service guide who brings the battlefield to life., following the course of the fighting while uncovering the stories of the soldiers who fought here and the families whose homes suddenly found themselves in the middle of history. With an expert guide bringing the landscape to life, you’ll discover how a quiet stretch of Maryland came to play an extraordinary role in the nation’s story. History happened here in a single day. The consequences took rather longer. DURATION: 1 hour DEPARTS FROM: Monocacy National Battlefield, 5201 Urbana Pike Frederick, MD 21704 TICKETING DETAILS: $35 per person. A minimum total of 15 tickets must be sold for the tour to run. If we don’t sell the required minimum of tickets, we’ll gladly refund your purchase or credit it toward another exciting tour. We’re committed to ensuring you have a fantastic experience, and we appreciate your understanding as we work to create fun, unforgettable events together!

events.title: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power
events.description: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power, an exhibition examining the beauty, dynamism, and political force of collective Black life across the African Diaspora through the photography of Howard alumna Adreinne Waheed. Curated by Kathryn Coney-Ali, executive director of the Howard University Gallery of Art, and Dr. Melanee C. Harvey-Fryar, associate professor of art history in the Chadwick A. Boseman College of Fine Arts, the exhibition brings Waheed’s documentary street photography into conversation with selections from the Waheed Photo Archive. Together, the works explore Black joy, protest, community, cultural tradition, and the power created when people gather. Necessary Means opens Wednesday, October 14, 2026, at the Howard University Museum in Founders Library and remains on view through May 28, 2027.

events.description: NextStop Theatre presents The Elaborate Entrance of Chad Deity from November 5th–29th, 2026, at 269 Sunset Park Drive in Herndon, Fairfax County, Virginia. This Pulitzer Prize-finalist comedy by Kristoffer Diaz body-slams the world of pro-wrestling, pop culture, and the performance of identity. Told through the eyes of Macedonio "The Mace" Guerra, a gifted wrestler stuck being paid to lose to a bigger-named star in the ring, this knockout satire takes on cultural stereotypes, media spectacle, and the courage it takes to say no. A bold, tour-de-force comedy that leaves it all on the mat! Directed by Stefan Sittig, a multi-disciplined theatre veteran with 140+ productions across New York City, international venues, and D.C.-area theaters, the production features Sittig's expertise as a Helen Hayes Award-nominated director, choreographer, and fight director. Kristoffer Diaz, the playwright and screenwriter, is also known for his musical Hell's Kitchen (created with Alicia Keys), nominated for 13 Tony Awards and currently running on Broadway. Audience advisories include strong language, simulated violence/fighting, racial stereotypes, and flashing lights and haze effects. The 2nd Sunday matinee will be a mask-required performance (masks provided). The Elaborate Entrance of Chad Deity combines theatrical excellence, sharp satire, and bold storytelling in Fairfax County, Virginia. events.title: Revolutionary Stories: Indigenous Americans and the American Revolution
events.description: James “Jay” G. Harrison III, Executive Director of The Museum of Culpeper History, historian, first person living history interpreter, and archaeologist will discuss the history of Indigenous Americans in the American Revolution. In particular, he will examine the alliances of Native nations: how they viewed the war, why some tribes remained neutral, why others chose the side of the American colonists and while still others allied themselves with the British. In addition, Mr. Harrison will discuss the roles and contributions of Indigenous Americans during this conflict as diplomats, scouts and soldiers. Event Details: Sunday, November 8, 2026 Program begins at 2:00 p.m. RSVP Required Revolutionary Stories is open to the public, and presentations will be uploaded to our YouTube channel. events.description: 8 performances | Oct. 31 and Nov. 6*, 7, 13 & 14 at 7:30 p.m. | Nov. 1, 8 & 15 at 2 p.m. Set in one of the most pivotal times in America’s history, the Tony-nominated Caroline, or Change is riveting, moving, and awe-inspiring. Featuring a virtuosic score by Jeanine Tesori (Shrek The Musical, Thoroughly Modern Millie), it blends blues, gospel and traditional Jewish melodies, creating a breathtaking medium for Kushner’s provocative and personal story. In 1963, the Gellman family and their African-American maid, Caroline, live in sleepy Lake Charles, Louisiana. Caroline is drifting through life as a single mother of four, working in a service job for a white family. A fragile, yet beautiful friendship develops between the young Gellman son, Noah, and Caroline. Noah’s stepmother, Rose, unable to give Caroline a raise, tells Caroline that she may keep the money that Noah leaves in his pockets. Caroline balks and refuses to take money from a child, but her own children desperately need food, clothing and shoes. Outside of the laundry room, some of the greatest social advancements that the country has seen are being set in motion, and change is knocking on the door. Caroline, or Change, produces a valuable theatrical experience that continues to thrill audiences the world over. It is a story that must be shared and will touch hearts. events.title: Shifting Boundaries: Perspectives on American Landscapes
events.address: Jefferson Drive at 12th St., SW, Washington, DC
events.description: American painters Willard Metcalf, Dwight Tryon, Winslow Homer, and Abbott Thayer created profoundly beautiful views of the New England landscapes where they lived and worked. These paintings largely depict that environment as timeless and static. Shifting Boundaries looks at these works from a new angle by engaging a multiplicity of voices and viewpoints to explore what these paintings can tell us about changes to this region both past and present. As Shifting Boundaries reveals, the views these artists created of pasturelands in Massachusetts and of seascapes in Maine were transforming even as these artists recorded them. This reshaping of landscapes has only accelerated in the century since Metcalf, Tryon, Homer, and Thayer depicted them. Shifting Boundaries pilots a new mode of collaborative curatorial practice. NMAA Lunder Curator of American Art Diana Greenwold , curatorial assistant Mary Mulcahy , and interpretation specialists Liz Gardner and Amy Freesun partnered with Lauren Brandes (Smithsonian Gardens), Dennis Chestnut (Groundwork Anacostia River DC), Jerome Foster II (Waic Up), Elizabeth James-Perry (Aquinnah Wampanoag artist), Lorette Picciano (Rural Coalition), Stephanie Toothman (National Park Service), and Melinda Whicher (Smithsonian Gardens) to develop the themes for this exhibition, select works of art, and write object labels. The group’s perspectives, drawn from their individual areas of professional expertise and their own personal experiences, allow us to see new details in these stunning works of art. The landscapes become invitations to explore a century of human impact on New England land and water, the erasure of indigenous histories, and the environmental changes that are altering this region today.

events.description: Learn about the role “sacred music” plays in the historical and contemporary relationship between Church and State during St. Anne's Episcopal Church’s Fall Adult Forum Lecture Series. The series, which examines the role of the Church in American political life, continues at 11:30 a.m. on Sunday, Nov. 8, at the church’s Parish Hall, 199 Duke of Gloucester St. in Annapolis, Md., The event is free and open to the public. J. Ernest Green, director of music and choirmaster at St. Anne's, and Larry Molinaro, the church’s associate director of music and its organist, will speak at the forum. The two are well known around Annapolis. Green has served as Live Arts Maryland’s artistic director for more than 40 years. He’s also music director of the Annapolis Chamber Orchestra and Annapolis Chorale. Molinaro serves as harpsichordist for the Annapolis Chorale and Chamber Orchestra and is co-director of the Bach+ series for St. Anne’s and Live Arts Maryland. The public is invited to attend this forum, and the next forum which will be held at 11:30 a.m. on Sunday, Nov. 15, at the Parish Hall. The Nov. 15 talk by the Rev. Dr. Manoj Mathew Zacharia, rector of St. Anne’s, will serve as the capstone of the eight-week Adult Forum series.

events.title: The 2026 Midterm Elections: Results, Implications, and the Political Road Ahead
events.venue: McLean Community Center, 1234 Ingleside Ave, McLean, VA 22101 703-790-0123
events.description: What Do the 2026 Midterm Elections Mean for America’s Political Future? Please join the AAUW McLean Area Branch for a special presentation by Stephen Farnsworth, PhD, Professor Emeritus of Political Science and International Affairs at the University of Mary Washington. Dr. Farnsworth will unpack the election results and will examine what they reveal about public opinion, the balance of power in Congress, and the future of the president’s policy agenda. Drawing on his expertise in American politics, presidential leadership, political communication, and Virginia politics, Dr. Farnsworth will explore how election outcomes may reshape relations between the White House and Congress, influence national policy debates, and set the stage for the 2028 presidential election. Dr. Farnsworth is a distinguished professor and the author or co-author of nine books on the presidency, mass media, public opinion, and journalism, and a recipient of Virginia’s Outstanding Faculty Award.

events.title: The American Story
events.description: The National Archives Museum debuts a once-in-a generation redesign of its permanent exhibits: The American Story and the Discovery Center - connecting visitors with the National Archives in revolutionary ways. The American Story will showcase items and records in the National Archives that tell important moments in our nation's history. Visitors will get up close to more than 40 original artifacts and documents, including a rare 1823 Stone Engraving of the Declaration of Independence, George Washington's annotated copy of the Constitution, and presidential gifts including horseshoes to President Bush from Queen Elizabeth II. The American Story will be the first and only museum in Washington, DC to use artificial intelligence (AI) to bring each visitor a special, individualized opportunity to explore the records of the American people and engage with American history. This exhibit brings more than two million historic records to life, offering a personalized journey through our nation's past. This new museum experience provides all Americans with a special opportunity to celebrate the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence.

events.title: The Art of Landscape: Beatrix Farrand's Enduring Imprint on Dumbarton Oaks
events.description: Beatrix Farrand is considered the first commercially successful woman landscape architect in the United States. Dumbarton Oaks Park in Georgetown is one of her lasting legacies. Come explore her creation with park rangers and learn how her design philosophy and unique vision helped shape this landscape, how that vision was nearly lost, and how the NPS and Dumbarton Oaks Park Conservancy are working to see that vision reimplemented today. Meet at the Dumbarton Oaks Park sign on R St. NW between 31 st St. NW and Avon Pl. NW. Walk may be cancelled in the event of bad weather at the discretion of park staff. Feel free to check the Rock Creek Park website the day of to confirm. Or call the Nature Center (202-895-6070) the day of to confirm and be sure to leave a voicemail for a callback.

events.title: We Make History
events.description: As the nation commemorates 250 years since the signing of the Declaration of Independence, "We Make History" explores how history happens, is preserved and shared. In Washington, D.C. and places around the country, many people were quietly keeping the records, building the collections, and developing the skills that would create America’s historical narrative. These community-based stories serve as the building blocks for 250 years of American history. Using the country’s anniversary as a milestone, the museum uses its community driven practice to celebrate local civic engagement and encourage local history keeping. This exhibition is a tribute to celebrating our communities and making possible a better understanding of our shared past. These stories are important to marking the Semiquincentennial because they help show the legacy of how people make history one act, one document, one story at a time. By bringing these stories to the forefront in 2026, the exhibit inspires the next generation to keep and share their own stories and records to add to America’s historical narrative. We Make History has an anticipated opening date of May 30, 2026.

events.title: "Inside Gaza" Film Screening & Discussion
events.description: The Institute for Middle East Studies is proud to announce a screening of the award winning documentary Inside Gaza, followed by remarks from film director Hélène Lam Trong and featured journalist Mai Yaghi. Since the Hamas attack on 7 October 2023 and the Israeli reprisals that followed, international journalists and media have no access to the Gaza Strip. Agence France-Presse journalists, who were permanently stationed in Gaza, were among the last independent witnesses to the abuses committed in the hellscape that Gaza has become. Featuring previously unseen footage and testimony from reporters Mai Yaghi and Adel Zaanoun, as well as photojournalists Mahmud Hams and Mohammed Abed, Inside Gaza delivers a powerful account of conditions on the ground, underscoring the vital importance of a free and independent press. All are invited to join the Institute for Middle East Studies for this film screening and discussion with film director Hélène Lam Trong and featured journalist Mai Yaghi. A trailer for the documentary can be found here. Speakers: Hélène Lam Trong is a French documentary filmmaker. Her 2023 documentary Daech, les enfants fantômes (ISIS, the Ghost Children) earned her the Albert Londres Prize for an audio-visual work. Independent since 2018, she worked for several years at Radio France then at France télévisions. In 2024, she directed Raqqa, l'ombre de Daech. Mai Yaghi is an Agence France-Presse (AFP) journalist and one of the protagonists of Inside Gaza. Ms. Yaghi

events.title: Beyond Discovery: Archaeology, Heritage and Partnership in the Galilee
events.description: Join the CCAS Department of Classical and Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations for a presentation on the U.S.-funded Galilee Heritage Project at Huqoq and Bethsaida. Focusing primarily on Huqoq, this lecture traces the journey from archaeological discovery to conservation, interpretation and public engagement, including new finds from 2026, the Secrets of Huqoq exhibition and new digital initiatives. Speaker: Dr. Shua Kisilevitz, Albright Institute of Archaeological Research and Tel Aviv University About the Project: What happens to an archaeological site after excavation ends, but long before it can open to the public? The Galilee Heritage Project addresses this challenge at two recently excavated sites near the Sea of Galilee, the late Roman synagogue and extraordinary mosaics of Huqoq and the Byzantine church at Bethsaida (El-Araj), identified by its excavators as the Church of the Apostles. Together, these exceptional discoveries offer compelling windows into the culturally and religiously diverse world of the Galilee in Late Antiquity. Led by the W. F. Albright Institute of Archaeological Research with U.S. federal support, the project also highlights the enduring role of American scholarship and American-Israeli institutional partnership in researching, preserving and sharing the region's archaeological heritage.

events.title: Book Seminar - Capitalism in South Korea, 1945-2025
events.description: How did South Korea’s rapid economic transformation shape its democracy, institutions, and society? In his book, Keun Lee examines South Korea’s development since 1945 through a framework of compressed development, decompression, and convergence. He explores how rapid growth helped create a middle class that demanded political freedom, and how IMF-led reforms following the Asian financial crisis reshaped the country’s economic trajectory. The seminar will examine the book's findings. Read a full abstract here. About the Speaker Keun Lee is a Distinguished Professor of Economics at Chung-Ang University and professor emeritus at Seoul National University. He is a fellow at the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research, founding director of the Center for Economic Catch-Up, and an editor of Research Policy. He obtained his PhD in economics from the University of California, Berkeley. Lee spent a year at the World Bank as a visiting scholar in 2004 and 2005, received the 2014 Schumpeter Prize for Schumpeterian Analysis of Economic Catch-up and served as vice-chairman of South Korea’s National Economic Advisory Council in 2021. His recent books include China’s Technological Leapfrogging and Economic Catch-up (2021) and Innovation–Development Detours for Latecomers (2024). Hosted by the Elliott School’s International Science and Technology Policy program, with co-sponsorship from the GW Institute for Korean Studies.

A career diplomat, Ambassador Varvuolis most recently served as ambassador-at-large at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Lithuania, where he led Lithuania’s work on regional connectivity and the Three Seas Initiative. He previously held ambassadorial postings to the Kingdom of Belgium (2013–2018) and Japan (2018–2021), with concurrent accreditation to several countries in Europe and the Asia-Pacific region. events.description: The Carter Center and GWSPH will host a screening of The President and the Dragon, a documentary chronicling President Jimmy Carter’s decades-long effort to eradicate Guinea worm disease. events.title: Research & Enrichment! Science with Your Dog
events.description: Join the GW Dog Lab for fun, free enrichment with your dog! The GW Canine Cognition Collaborative (aka GW Dog Lab) is a student-run lab in the Anthropology Department. Research sessions are on campus, after hours and on weekends, and are designed to last only 1 hour. Because humans and dogs share an environment, we can learn a lot about the way that environment has shaped our species by comparing dog and toddler cognition. We play simple games with dogs designed to measure their cognition and then compare them to toddlers. How to Participate 1. Start by submitting a pre-screening form. This helps us learn about your dog 2. Next, open your email and look for your onboarding information sent from canine.cognition@gwu.edu. 3. Then, using the information in your email, sign up for your initial visit. This is a get-to-know-you visit that makes it easier for dogs to get acclimated to our testing space. 4. Finally, after the initial visit, depending on your dog's comfort level, you will get email invitations to studies your dog is eligible for! Parking information can be found on the GW Dog Lab website.

events.title: Rick Steves
events.description: In the 1970s, the ultimate trip for any backpacker was the storied “Hippie Trail,” a 3,000-mile trek from Istanbul to Kathmandu. A 23-year-old Rick Steves made the trek in 1978, and like a travel writer in training, he documented everything along the way: jumping off a moving train, making friends in Tehran, getting lost in Lahore, getting high for the first time in Herat, battling leeches in Pokhara, and more. The experience ignited his love of travel and forever broadened his perspective on the world. On the Hippie Trail: Istanbul to Kathmandu and the Making of a Travel Writer —a New York Times bestseller now out in paperback—contains edited selections from Rick Steves’ journal and travel photos with a 45-years-later preface and postscript reflecting on how his journey through Turkey, Iran, Afghanistan, Pakistan, India, and Nepal changed his life.

events.title: A Virtual Lecture from Historic Annapolis – William and Dinah Nuthead: Maryland’s First Printers
events.description: Before Jonas and Anne Catharine Hoof Green, there was William and Dinah Nuthead, Maryland’s first printing duo. William Nuthead was the first printer in Maryland and the first to operate a press in Virginia, establishing his business in St. Mary’s City in 1685 after being barred from printing in Virginia by the colonial government. Following his death in 1695, his widow Dinah Nuthead took over the business and became the first licensed female printer in the American colonies. Join Rod Cofield as he discusses his research into their lives that led to his Maryland Historical Magazine article, “Much Ado about Nuthead.” The Historic Annapolis Virtual Lecture Series is offered free of charge thanks to the generosity of an anonymous donor. If you enjoy this program, we hope you will consider becoming a member or making a donation today to support Historic Annapolis and our mission to connect all people with our shared history. Can’t watch live? All lectures will be recorded. Please register and you’ll receive the link to watch the recording after the event. Advance registration required; registration closes on half-hour prior to lecture. Cost: FREE This lecture will be offered virtually by Zoom. Upon registration, you will be sent the link for the video conference to join on the evening of the lecture. If you do not receive your confirmation email after you register, please check your Spam folder, or email Cara Garside at cara.garside@annapolis.org . To learn more about Zoom and to download the app to your computer, visit the Zoom website . About Our Presenter: Rod Cofield is the Executive Director at Jefferson Patterson Park and Museum in Calvert County. events.title: Book Talk- Caring Like a State: The Politics of Russia's Demographic Crisis
events.description: The post-Soviet Russian state has long been haunted by the specter of a dwindling population. Since the dissolution of the Soviet Union, and despite well-publicized pro-natalist campaigns, the population has continued to contract, raising doubts about the state’s capacity to care effectively for its citizens. The talk draws on Inna Leykin's book Caring Like a State: The Politics of Russia's Demographic Crisis that explores the national preoccupation with demography from the dissolution of the Soviet Union to the full-scale invasion of sovereign Ukraine. Moving beyond policy analysis, it focuses on the role of socio-demographic knowledge in shaping how the state defines social problems, identifies target populations, and determines who should be the object of state care and intervention. By tracing the circulation of demographic knowledge across expert communities, state institutions, and everyday life, the book shows how the “demographic crisis” has been socially organized and how responses to it generate alternative understandings and practices of care that do not always align with state visions. The discussion will be moderated by Ivan Grek, Director of the Russia Program.

events.title: Forgiveness: Grace in the Messiness of Being Human
events.description: Forgiveness is far more complicated than a simple spiritual decision. Drawing on theology, psychology, and physical well-being, this Taproom Theology conversation explores the grace we receive and the forgiveness we extend, while making room for the anger, grief, regret, and unresolved hurt that shape our lives and relationships. Together, we’ll wrestle with the tensions between grace and accountability, forgiveness and boundaries, and healing and reconciliation. We’ll consider why forgiveness doesn’t mean excusing harm, forgetting what happened, or returning to unsafe relationships, and how God’s love meets us not just when we forgive, but throughout the messy, imperfect process of getting there. Join Taproom Theology for an insightful evening featuring Sage Bolte, PhD, a renowned educator and mental health therapist. Explore the complex themes of grace and forgiveness within a relaxed atmosphere where beliefs are brewed and hope is on tap.

events.title: LEE EMI (Emilee Petersmark of The Crane Wives)
Life of Courage: Bruce McCandless and the Pacific War
events.venue: U.S. Naval Institute's Jack C. Taylor Conference Center
events.description: Join the U.S. Naval Institute on 10 November 2026 at 10:30 AM ET at the Jack C. Taylor Conference Center, in Annapolis, MD for a look inside the new book Iron and Fire: The Pacific War Story of Destroyer Captain Bruce McCandless with Bruce McCandless III as he recounts his grandfather’s—Admiral Bruce McCandless—wartime experiences across the Pacific. Lieutenant Bruce McCandless was at Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941, fought aboard the heavy cruiser USS San Francisco (CA 38) through the brutal Guadalcanal campaign. Later promoted to captain, he commanded the destroyer USS Gregory (DD 802) during the final drive across the Pacific. Late in life, retiring as an admiral, he dictated his wartime memories to his daughter Sue; the manuscript was then set aside for many years. Iron and Fire draws on family letters, photographs, shipmates’ recollections, and stories passed down through generations to share his story. Due to the requirements of the U.S. Naval Academy and the timing of this event, in person attendance is only open to U.S. citizens. events.title: Ted Scheinman for Jolt: My Electric Journey Out of Darkness
events.description: Growing up in a hyper-educated, artistic, eccentric family, Ted Scheinman, the son of a medical doctor and an English professor, spent much of his precocious childhood as a writer and performer—and his greatest performance was as someone who was happy. He recognized his depression early and recorded its effects in a series of tragicomic journals, always hoping that the ritual of doing so would palliate if not cure. While the clouds occasionally parted, particularly during Ted’s years of intellectual questing at Hotchkiss and Yale—and, fleetingly, through his emergence as a successful journalist—his gloom kept returning, seemingly more debilitating each time. Eventually, a series of emotional plunges deposited Ted, at age thirty-five, in a psych ward in Washington, DC. There, he began an intensive course of electroconvulsive therapy—considered by most a treatment of last resort. The controversial procedure saved his life, but it also exacted a price: he was now missing important pieces of his memory. By turns deeply gripping, startlingly perceptive, understatedly hilarious, and heartbreakingly poignant, particularly in Ted’s depiction of his romantic relationships, Jolt asks: How do our families shape who we are, for good and ill? How much of our character is ingrained versus sculpted by circumstances? How can we adapt when our memory fails? Perhaps most critically: What are we willing to sacrifice to have a chance at life? events.title: Virtual Lecture – William and Dinah Nuthead: Maryland’s First Printers
events.description: Before Jonas and Anne Catharine Hoof Green, there was William and Dinah Nuthead, Maryland’s first printing duo. William Nuthead was the first printer in Maryland and the first to operate a press in Virginia, establishing his business in St. Mary’s City in 1685 after being barred from printing in Virginia by the colonial government. Following his death in 1695, his widow Dinah Nuthead took over the business and became the first licensed female printer in the American colonies. Join Rod Cofield as he discusses his research into their lives that led to his Maryland Historical Magazine article, “Much Ado about Nuthead.” The Historic Annapolis Virtual Lecture Series is offered free of charge thanks to the generosity of an anonymous donor. If you enjoy this program, we hope you will consider becoming a member or making a donation today to support Historic Annapolis and our mission to connect all people with our shared history. Can’t watch live? All lectures will be recorded. Please register and you’ll receive the link to watch the recording after the event. events.title: A Gift in Motion
events.description: A multidisciplinary showcase from the artists and scholars of the full-time faculty and staff at the Corcoran School of the Arts & Design. A Gift In Motion loosely draws from Robin Wall Kimmerer’s book The Serviceberry which uplifts Indigenous frameworks of the natural world to advance the possibilities in collectivity, reciprocity, and the mindset of abundance. These are anti-capitalist models and theories that provide insight into the systems of power we negotiate, but also offer a lens on how we individually move through our daily lives—together—through historically fraught landscapes. A keen reminder that working with, for, and because of each other remains the most human motivation, even while we are inundated with narratives that suggest otherwise. Within the walls of the academy, frameworks of artistic and creative knowledge are often dismissed, as are Indigenous methodologies and community-focused perspectives that center human engagement, oral and craft-based practices, and unquantifiable research. A personal experience. A feeling. Abstraction. And yet, for centuries, within the walls of art schools exist myriad economies of imagination that are anchored in the sharing of diverse creative knowledge and articulated in what we make, write, perform, dance, build, conserve, collect, display, speak, and think. events.title: Camp One Heartland
events.description: Camp One Heartland is a solo exhibition by Tye DuSold-O’Connor archiving documentation of one of the world’s first nonprofit summer camps designated to supporting and empowering youth affected by HIV and AIDS, eventually transforming into a vital beacon of safety, liberation and eutopia for LGBTQ+ youth across the country. After its inaugural session in the summer of 1993 and many more held at different campsites across the country, Camp One Heartland found its permanent residence in Willow River, Minnesota. Over the next three decades it broadened its reach to provide summer camp sessions for youth experiencing housing instability, LGBTQ+ youth, and specifically trans youth. Tye attended Camp One Heartland as both a camper in 2022 and a counselor in 2024, and found these experiences indescribably transformative to them and their queer identity. Quite suddenly, Camp One Heartland shut down permanently in the fall of 2024 due to financial issues. Former campers, counselors and staff have been unable to return to the site since. While camp counseling in the summer of 2024, Tye took hundreds of photos of the camp, its people, and its experiences. These serve as some of the last images taken during the lifetime of Camp One Heartland. Artist Bio: Tye DuSold-O’Connor is a multimedia artist studying Fine Art and Psychology whose work revolves around trans experience, identity and culture. events.title: Cannupa Hanska Luger’s REFLECT
events.description: REFLECT traces the evolution of artist Cannuap Hanska Luger’s Mirror Shield Project. In 2016, when the Dakota Access Pipeline threatened the waters of his ancestral homelands, Luger circulated a video demonstrating how to make “mirror shields” from inexpensive materials. Conceived during the Indigenous-led resistance at Standing Rock, North Dakota, the tutorial functioned as a call to collective action, an invitation for people across the country to stand in solidarity with the Water Protectors. Carried by Water Protectors in frontline actions and collective formations, the mirrored surfaces offered protection while redirecting the field of vision. More than a thousand mirror shields were created and transported to the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ camp. The exhibition brings the project’s history into the present, treating the archive as a resource to be carried forward and put into practice. Photographs, videos, garments, ephemera, and community-generated documentation reveal a collective artwork shaped by those who made, carried, adapted, interpreted, and activated it.

events.title: Cracks & Reforms: The 1920s Through the GW Collection
events.description: The 1920s emerged as a decade suspended between collapse and reconstruction, an era marked by “cracks and reforms” that ushered in a profound reconfiguration of the visual world. During this period marked by civil transformation and political upheaval, artists, journalists, and makers had opportunities to reconstruct both individual and collective identities. A century later, Cracks & Reforms presents a distinct cross-section of this period, revealing global currents of migration, modernization, and cultural redefinition through the lens of the GW Collection. Students led by Associate Professor Bibiana Obler selected works to study and exhibit, their research eventually leading to unified themes and a catalog designed by Corcoran graphic design students led by professors Sharmila Karamchandani and Aasawari Kulkarni. Image: Boris Ignatovich (Russian, 1899-1976), Composer Dmitri Shostakovich, from "Ignatovich, Soviet Avant-Garde", 1928, gelatin silver print, 16 H x 20 W in. events.title: Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY
events.description: For Freedoms presents artist and educator Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY which centers on Ethiopian journalist and author Baalu Girma’s controversial 1984 Amharic novel Oromay, written under the Derg regime and banned shortly after its publication. Drawing on Gottesman’s deep engagement with the novel, NIGHT AND DAY considers how artists create, communicate, and sustain cultural memory within and against conditions of censorship, political repression, and state violence. The exhibition extends beyond the gallery through a library of banned books, a self-guided workshop station that invites visitors to respond to censorship through writing and drawing, and a public conversation on how artists sustain creative practice amid sociopolitical pressure.

events.title: Israel’s Existential Election: A Conversation with Dr. Dahlia Scheindlin
events.description: On October 27th, Israeli citizens went to the polls for the first time since the October 7th, 2023 Hamas attack and the years of war that have followed in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. Dr. Dahlia Scheindlin, Israel's foremost public opinion expert, will analyze the complex results of this fateful election and their implications for Israel, conflict with the Palestinians, relations with the US and regional politics. The Elliott School's Ned Lazarus will moderate. Dr. Dahlia Scheindlin is a public opinion expert and political strategist who has advised national campaigns in Israel and fifteen other countries. Dahlia is a Senior Analyst and columnist for Haaretz. Her book, The Crooked Timber of Democracy in Israel: Promise Unfulfilled was listed on Foreign Affairs' Best Books of 2024. Dahlia conducts extensive public opinion research for civil society organizations, including joint Israeli-Palestinian surveys. Her writing has appeared in The New York Times, The Guardian, The Observer, Foreign Affairs, Foreign Policy, Financial Times, Time Magazine, The New York Review of Books, The New Statesman, and The New York Post. Dr. Ned Lazarus is Teaching Associate Professor of International Affairs at the Elliott School and an Israel Institute Teaching Fellow. A Conflict Resolution scholar, practitioner and evaluator, Ned has conducted evaluative studies of peacebuilding initiatives on behalf of USAID, USIP, the European Union and the US Department of State. events.title: Korea Policy Forum- Recalibrating Northeast Asian Geopolitics after the U.S. Midterms
events.description: The 2026 U.S. midterm elections will set the political landscape in Washington for the remainder of President Trump’s second term, with important implications for U.S. policy toward Northeast Asia. At the same time, shifting U.S.–China relations, developments on the Korean Peninsula, and growing economic and technological competition are adding new uncertainties to the regional order. This Korea Policy Forum brings together leading experts from the United States and South Korea to assess the post-midterm outlook for Northeast Asia from both Washington and Seoul perspectives. Following a keynote address on South Korea’s strategic choices, the discussion will examine regional security, the U.S.–ROK alliance, U.S.–China relations, and emerging challenges in trade, technology, and economic security. The GW Institute for Korean Studies invites you to join this timely and forward-looking discussion.

events.title: LeVar Burton
events.description: Tracing the different eras of his life—from “Roots” to “Star Trek: The Next Generation” to “Reading Rainbow” and far beyond the camera—actor LeVar Burton fearlessly opens up about growing up during the Civil Rights Movement, being raised by a remarkable mother, and discovering his calling as a storyteller in Take My Word for It. He explores how acting has served as both a source of transformation and an escape from the most difficult parts of his past, while also confronting the challenges of being a parent, husband, and householder. As Burton honors the loved ones whose strength and resilience shaped him, he also asks what we owe to our ancestors and to each other, reflecting on the deep necessity he’s always felt to advocate for liberation and equity. Burton will be in conversation with Michele Norris, a Peabody and Emmy Award-winning journalist, the host of the podcast “ Your Mama’s Kitchen,” and the author of Our Hidden Conversations: What Americans Really Think About Race and Identity.

events.title: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power
events.description: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power, an exhibition examining the beauty, dynamism, and political force of collective Black life across the African Diaspora through the photography of Howard alumna Adreinne Waheed. Curated by Kathryn Coney-Ali, executive director of the Howard University Gallery of Art, and Dr. Melanee C. Harvey-Fryar, associate professor of art history in the Chadwick A. Boseman College of Fine Arts, the exhibition brings Waheed’s documentary street photography into conversation with selections from the Waheed Photo Archive. Together, the works explore Black joy, protest, community, cultural tradition, and the power created when people gather. Necessary Means opens Wednesday, October 14, 2026, at the Howard University Museum in Founders Library and remains on view through May 28, 2027.

events.title: The Civil War
events.description: From 1861 to 1865, Americans fought each other with a ferocity unseen in the country’s history. The immediate cause of the war was the secession of the Southern states. However, the roots lay in growing tensions over slavery. By the time the last shots were fired, as many as 750,000 Americans had been killed, and four million enslaved people were freed. This traveling banner exhibition, from the Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History, examines the impact of the Civil War on Americans throughout the fractured nation. The exhibit will be on display at the Fairfax Museum and Visitor Center (10209 Main St.) from November 11 - December 4. Discover More Attractions in #FXVA

events.title: A Gift in Motion
events.description: A multidisciplinary showcase from the artists and scholars of the full-time faculty and staff at the Corcoran School of the Arts & Design. A Gift In Motion loosely draws from Robin Wall Kimmerer’s book The Serviceberry which uplifts Indigenous frameworks of the natural world to advance the possibilities in collectivity, reciprocity, and the mindset of abundance. These are anti-capitalist models and theories that provide insight into the systems of power we negotiate, but also offer a lens on how we individually move through our daily lives—together—through historically fraught landscapes. A keen reminder that working with, for, and because of each other remains the most human motivation, even while we are inundated with narratives that suggest otherwise. Within the walls of the academy, frameworks of artistic and creative knowledge are often dismissed, as are Indigenous methodologies and community-focused perspectives that center human engagement, oral and craft-based practices, and unquantifiable research. A personal experience. A feeling. Abstraction. And yet, for centuries, within the walls of art schools exist myriad economies of imagination that are anchored in the sharing of diverse creative knowledge and articulated in what we make, write, perform, dance, build, conserve, collect, display, speak, and think. Art Capital: Museum Politics and the Making of the Louvre Abu Dhabi
events.description: Attend In-Person or Attend Online The Institute for Middle East Studies, in-partnership with the Corcoran School of the Arts and Design, invites you to join author Beth Derderian and discussant Joshua Bell for an exploration of Art Capital: Museum Politics and the Making of the Louvre Abu Dhabi. Museums often served nationalist and imperialist interests in the past, but the primary force in the 21st century is the market. Museum franchising—exemplified by the Louvre Abu Dhabi—is one of the most visible cases of the increasing entanglement of art and museums with capital interests. Such projects are often touted as global enterprises diversifying the art world. Frequently, critics of these controversial projects question these claims and market influence. The intersection of these two forces—increasing capitalization and moving toward inclusivity—creates a fundamental tension, and that is the subject of Beth Derderian's Art Capital. Focusing on the decade between the Louvre Abu Dhabi's announcement and its eventual opening, the book analyzes how major shifts away from the 19th- and 20th-century paradigm of culture-state representation play out in museums' and artists' everyday practices. Dr. Derderian traces the emergence of a new logic, wherein the ways that artists represent the state shift, as does the notion of what constitutes 'good art.' In addition, these intersecting forces spur preemptive erasures that neutralize and depoliticize difference for museum publics. Drawing

events.title: Art Opening Jane Kell: Coastal
events.description: Come join us at Amy Kaslow Gallery for the opening reception of Jane Kell: Coastal Jane Kell returns this fall with a new body of immersive work, a collection of eleven oil paintings and fifteen works on paper. We’re excited to welcome this leading British artist back to the gallery for her fifth exhibition with us. Amy Kaslow Gallery and Jane Kell have been together since we opened in 2020. Kell was our first artist-in-residence, always accompanied by her loyal rescue dog, Penny. The two moved back to London where the painter built a bright and expansive studio. An avid traveler to the countryside and the water’s edge, she is drawn to these natural vistas, raw and untouched. In this series of paintings powerful tones and graceful forms bleed and fuse elegantly. Brilliant, bold, and saturated, the cavernous Arcadian Landscape and Canyon command any room. Both much larger than Kell's earlier abstracts, Kell created these expansive vistas on unstretched canvases pinned to the studio wall. This is a method Kell first used in 2020 for her debut show with the gallery and she has since found it a way to be free and experimental.

events.title: Camp One Heartland
events.description: Camp One Heartland is a solo exhibition by Tye DuSold-O’Connor archiving documentation of one of the world’s first nonprofit summer camps designated to supporting and empowering youth affected by HIV and AIDS, eventually transforming into a vital beacon of safety, liberation and eutopia for LGBTQ+ youth across the country. After its inaugural session in the summer of 1993 and many more held at different campsites across the country, Camp One Heartland found its permanent residence in Willow River, Minnesota. Over the next three decades it broadened its reach to provide summer camp sessions for youth experiencing housing instability, LGBTQ+ youth, and specifically trans youth. Tye attended Camp One Heartland as both a camper in 2022 and a counselor in 2024, and found these experiences indescribably transformative to them and their queer identity. Quite suddenly, Camp One Heartland shut down permanently in the fall of 2024 due to financial issues. Former campers, counselors and staff have been unable to return to the site since. While camp counseling in the summer of 2024, Tye took hundreds of photos of the camp, its people, and its experiences. These serve as some of the last images taken during the lifetime of Camp One Heartland. events.title: Cannupa Hanska Luger’s REFLECT
events.description: REFLECT traces the evolution of artist Cannuap Hanska Luger’s Mirror Shield Project. In 2016, when the Dakota Access Pipeline threatened the waters of his ancestral homelands, Luger circulated a video demonstrating how to make “mirror shields” from inexpensive materials. Conceived during the Indigenous-led resistance at Standing Rock, North Dakota, the tutorial functioned as a call to collective action, an invitation for people across the country to stand in solidarity with the Water Protectors. Carried by Water Protectors in frontline actions and collective formations, the mirrored surfaces offered protection while redirecting the field of vision. More than a thousand mirror shields were created and transported to the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ camp. The exhibition brings the project’s history into the present, treating the archive as a resource to be carried forward and put into practice. Photographs, videos, garments, ephemera, and community-generated documentation reveal a collective artwork shaped by those who made, carried, adapted, interpreted, and activated it.

events.title: Cracks & Reforms: The 1920s Through the GW Collection
events.description: The 1920s emerged as a decade suspended between collapse and reconstruction, an era marked by “cracks and reforms” that ushered in a profound reconfiguration of the visual world. During this period marked by civil transformation and political upheaval, artists, journalists, and makers had opportunities to reconstruct both individual and collective identities. A century later, Cracks & Reforms presents a distinct cross-section of this period, revealing global currents of migration, modernization, and cultural redefinition through the lens of the GW Collection. Students led by Associate Professor Bibiana Obler selected works to study and exhibit, their research eventually leading to unified themes and a catalog designed by Corcoran graphic design students led by professors Sharmila Karamchandani and Aasawari Kulkarni. Image: Boris Ignatovich (Russian, 1899-1976), Composer Dmitri Shostakovich, from "Ignatovich, Soviet Avant-Garde", 1928, gelatin silver print, 16 H x 20 W in. events.title: Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY
events.description: For Freedoms presents artist and educator Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY which centers on Ethiopian journalist and author Baalu Girma’s controversial 1984 Amharic novel Oromay, written under the Derg regime and banned shortly after its publication. Drawing on Gottesman’s deep engagement with the novel, NIGHT AND DAY considers how artists create, communicate, and sustain cultural memory within and against conditions of censorship, political repression, and state violence. The exhibition extends beyond the gallery through a library of banned books, a self-guided workshop station that invites visitors to respond to censorship through writing and drawing, and a public conversation on how artists sustain creative practice amid sociopolitical pressure.

events.title: Giles Corey
events.description: First released in 2011, the self-titled Giles Corey album began with a simple constraint: acoustic instruments only. That boundary opened into something much larger—guitar, piano, ghostly choirs, heavy organ, field recordings, and sudden walls of sound arranged around an intimate singer-songwriter core. The songs move through depression, death, history, and the paranormal without treating any of them as distant ideas. Quiet desperation gives way to cathartic outburst; private confession becomes communal release. The album and its accompanying book have since gathered a fervent following, often described by listeners in the language of ritual or religious experience. For the 2026–27 live set, Barrett brings that tension to the stage: stark voice and acoustic instruments, unstable electronics, and arrangements built to move from a whisper to physical impact. Kathryn Mohr is a Bay Area artist releasing music on The Flenser. events.title: Mental Reset: Sound Bath + Reiki : Thursday Evenings in Falls Church
events.address: 7777 Leesburg Pike, Ste 204S, Falls Church, VA 22043
events.description: Thursday is a weird day. The week isn't over, but you are. Mental Reset is one hour at the end of the workday where nobody needs anything from you. You come in, you lie down on a mat, you get a blanket and a bolster, and for the next sixty minutes your only job is to listen. I play crystal singing bowls, guide you through a short meditation so your mind has something to do besides replay the day, and offer Reiki while you rest. Most people tell me some version of the same thing afterward: the noise in their head finally turned down. Not off: down. Enough that they can go home and actually be home, instead of answering emails in their head at the dinner table. You don't need experience. You don't need to know how to meditate, and you definitely don't need to “clear your mind.” If you could do that, you wouldn't need this class. First-timers are in the room most weeks. There are ten spots. That's deliberate. It's a small room, I can see everyone in it, and it never feels like an event. It feels like an exhale. A few regulars started as skeptics; more than one of our Google reviews comes from someone who arrived doubting the whole thing and left surprised at how settled they felt. You don't have to believe in anything for an hour of sound and rest to do you some good. Run by Victoria Vita: CPA for 20+ years, healer for 7+. I sat behind a desk with a brain that wouldn't switch off for a long time before I found this work. Thursday nights are built for the person I used to be. Rated 5.0 from 32 Google reviews. Come straight from work. Leave like the week let go of you first. What's included: • 60 minutes of crystal singing bowls, guided meditation and Reiki • Mat, blanket, and bolster everything is here; you bring nothing • Small group: 10 people maximum, same teacher every week • Time at the end to sit up slowly, have water, and not rush out Discover More Attractions in #FXVA

events.description: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power, an exhibition examining the beauty, dynamism, and political force of collective Black life across the African Diaspora through the photography of Howard alumna Adreinne Waheed. Curated by Kathryn Coney-Ali, executive director of the Howard University Gallery of Art, and Dr. Melanee C. Harvey-Fryar, associate professor of art history in the Chadwick A. Boseman College of Fine Arts, the exhibition brings Waheed’s documentary street photography into conversation with selections from the Waheed Photo Archive. Together, the works explore Black joy, protest, community, cultural tradition, and the power created when people gather. Necessary Means opens Wednesday, October 14, 2026, at the Howard University Museum in Founders Library and remains on view through May 28, 2027.

events.title: Religion in Asia: Women's Rights and Religious Conversion Laws in India
events.description: In India, Hindu nationalists are curtailing women's rights through accusations that Muslim men are engaged in "love jihad"--a conspiracy to convert women into Muslims by seduction. The new laws in various Indian states penalize interfaith marriage between Muslims or Christians and Hindus. Some states require notifying the government of religious conversion 60 to 90 days in advance. Other regulations assume that marriage with a woman or minority community member who has converted is under coercion. These laws allow family members to file complaints about voluntary marriages, leading to arrests and government harassment. These laws assume that women have no agency and are only involved in interfaith marriage because they have been manipulated. Many families are willing to use the new laws to stop their daughters from entering a marriage that hasn't been family approved. This discussion will look at the new laws and how they are being implemented to restrict women's rights in India.

events.title: Research & Enrichment! Science with Your Dog
events.description: Join the GW Dog Lab for fun, free enrichment with your dog! The GW Canine Cognition Collaborative (aka GW Dog Lab) is a student-run lab in the Anthropology Department. Research sessions are on campus, after hours and on weekends, and are designed to last only 1 hour. Because humans and dogs share an environment, we can learn a lot about the way that environment has shaped our species by comparing dog and toddler cognition. We play simple games with dogs designed to measure their cognition and then compare them to toddlers. How to Participate 1. Start by submitting a pre-screening form. This helps us learn about your dog 2. Next, open your email and look for your onboarding information sent from canine.cognition@gwu.edu. 3. Then, using the information in your email, sign up for your initial visit. This is a get-to-know-you visit that makes it easier for dogs to get acclimated to our testing space. 4. Finally, after the initial visit, depending on your dog's comfort level, you will get email invitations to studies your dog is eligible for! Parking information can be found on the GW Dog Lab website.

events.title: The Maryland 1864 Constitution: A Border State’s Soldiers Stand for Freedom
events.description: Join Peerless Rockville as we mark Maryland Emancipation Day and Veterans Day with psychiatrist and author Dr. Stephen A. Goldman. In this presentation, he will discuss the 1864 Maryland Constitutional Election that emancipated enslaved Marylanders, the only state in the Union to end slavery through the state consititution. The soldiers’ vote in Maryland would greatly determine the state’s future, and their overwhelming support for slavery’s abolition exemplified how the war radicalized so many white servicemen throughout the Union. Of all the states involved in the Civil War, Maryland epitomized its harsh “brother against brother” reality, and the complicated prewar circumstances of slavery and freedom. While a border slave state, Maryland remained in the Union, and contributed 63,000 soldiers, sailors, and marines to its war effort, including ten thousand African Americans. By 1864, the state had reached a crossroads that the entire nation was confronting – a Civil War that had turned savage, whether Abraham Lincoln would be re-elected, and what would be the fate of four million human beings held in bondage. On November 1, 1864, the Maryland electorate voted to end slavery in the state. ABOUT THE SPEAKER Stephen A. events.title: 1776, the Musical, presented by The Pickwick Players
events.description: Virginia helped shape the beginnings of our nation, and local audiences can experience the drama, humor and music behind America’s founding in 1776 , the Tony Award-winning musical presented by The Pickwick Players. Just in time for America’s 250th anniversary, 1776 takes audiences inside the Continental Congress, where John Adams pushes for independence, Benjamin Franklin brings his wit and wisdom, and Virginia’s own Thomas Jefferson is called upon to put the revolutionary cause into words. The story also features Richard Henry Lee of Virginia, whose resolution calling for independence helped move the colonies toward a historic decision. What happens when a room full of passionate, stubborn and politically divided men try to agree on the future of a nation? There’s plenty of debate, a little scheming, larger-than-life personalities and some unforgettable music. With music and lyrics by Sherman Edwards and a book by Peter Stone, 1776 combines clever dialogue, colorful characters, political maneuvering and a memorable score. From the spirited opening number, “Sit Down, John,” to the lively “The Lees of Old Virginia” and the stirring “Is Anybody There?,” the music captures the humor, frustrations and high stakes behind the birth of a nation. Forget the dusty history books. 1776 presents the founding fathers as real people, with big egos, strong opinions, competing interests and a monumental decision to make. Recognized by the legal profession and honored with George Mason University's Jack Wood Award for Town-Gown Collaboration, Jazz4Justice has become a model for meaningful community engagement. In partnership with Legal Services of Northern Virginia, proceeds from this concert help provide free civil legal assistance to low-income individuals and families facing issues such as housing, domestic violence, consumer protection, family law, veterans' services, and public benefits. Through volunteer attorneys and dedicated legal advocates, LSNV works every day to help ensure that justice is not determined by one's ability to pay.
